newsitem.title: GERMANY: German liquidators cut three quarters of Sket jobs.
newsitem.headline: German liquidators cut three quarters of Sket jobs.

text.p: Troubled east German machinery company Sket GmbH must cut three-quarters of its workforce under an agreement reached on Tuesday between the officials charged with liquidating the firm.

Wolfgang Wutzke -- the lawyer charged with handling the liquidation of Sket -- and the BVS state agency agreed that Sket would be split into five separate rescue companies with a total of 425 employees from January 2.
But Sket's works committee and the huge German metals and engineering union IG Metall complained that the decision had not been put to a vote of the company's 1,850 workers.

Sket, which once employed 18,000 workers as a main supplier to communist eastern Europe, has soaked up billions in state aid after posting heavy losses since German unification. Wutzke said Sket was losing half a million marks per work day.
In mid-October, the firm filed for liquidation proceedings after its workforce refused to support a drastic cost-cutting programme which would have cut the workforce by two-thirds.
BVS said there was only buying interest for the individual businesses and not for Sket as a whole and said it had given out between 200 and 300 million marks for the plan.
BVS committee member Rudolf Bohn said the social provisions for the redundancies would alone come to between 75 and 90 million marks.
BVS will take on the initial losses of the rescue businesses, which Sket said should have a year's turnover of 130 million marks in total and make profits from 1998.
Bohn said a work society would be set up for 1,450 workers, which would secure work until the end of 1997 and said they would also receive three months' pay.
He also said all trainee contracts would be honoured.
Bohn added that the security of now threatened suppiers of Sket was still being dealt with.
According to finance minister for Saxony and Anhalt Klaus Schucht more than 60 Sket suppliers have already registered their concern for their own survial.
The plans now need the agreement of the German government and the European Commission.
The company's troubles made headline news in Germany, with the Bonn government coming under fire from the opposition Social Democrat Party for going back on promises to save Sket.
